newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rigid Germany threatens EMU - French central banker.
newsitem.headline: Rigid Germany threatens EMU - French central banker.

text.p: Bank of France member Jean-Pierre Gerard said on Thursday that devaluation of the French currency against the mark was undesirable but possibly necessary because of German incomprehension on monetary and exchange rate policy.

Gerard also said that Italy should be in on the creation of a euro single currency and bluntly accused Germany of resisting a country which had founded the European Union with France and Germany and which should be with them in launching the euro.
"There's a problem of loyalty to history. (Italy) wanted the construction of Europe, with the Germans and the French. It would be a mistake to create the euro without them," he said.
"At the time of Italy's re-entry into the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) (on Sunday), Germany gave too much the impression that it did not want Italy," he said.

Gerard, a member of the independent central bank's monetary policy council and believed to be one of a minority in favour of less stringent monetary policy within the Bank's inner sanctum, laid out his views in an interview in Le Monde newspaper.

The problem for EU countries was an "aggressive" U.S. trade policy based on an undervalued dollar, but German satisfaction with the dollar's level and the absence of French influence on its neighbour's monetary policy meant the option of changing franc-mark parity had to be considered, Gerard said.

His remarks drew a speedy rebuke from Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, who said the Bank of France's job was to preserve price stability and that members of the monetary policy council should keep misgivings to themselves rather than vent them in public.
"Each time the franc depreciates, (interest) rates go up. We want rates to go down," Arthuis said on LCI television.

Gerard's stark appraisal of German policy came days after similar comments by Paul Marchelli, seen as a minority ally of Gerard in the Bank's council, and declarations in a similar vein by former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing that revived debate over a decade-old policy of a strong currency tied to the mark.

"I think it's natural in a democratic system to worry about the future of our country. That's what he (Giscard d'Estaing) is talking about when he questions the franc-mark parity and, above all, the parity between the franc and the dollar," Gerard said.
"It is all the more worthwhile in that I believe that the Germans are not sufficiently aware of the problems which their monetary policy can have on the launch of the single currency."
Although Germany was satisfied with the current dollar rate, for France the correct parity was around six francs per dollar -- compared with 5.20 francs now, he said.
One way to get the dollar higher would be to cut short-term interest rates in France and Germany. "Unfortunately we have little influence on German monetary policy," he said.
"A second possibility, given that we cannot get a concerted reduction in rates, would be to modify the franc-mark parity. That is the reasoning of Monsieur Giscard d'Estaing."
"It is probably a less good solution since we are already overcompetitive compared to Germany, but German lack of understanding may make it necessary," he said.
Gerard said franc devaluation would "probably not" carry an inflation risk. Depreciation of the franc against the mark was not desirable, since this would increase market interest rates.
"Nevertheless, there is an optimum balance to be found between interest rates and exchange rates. This has not, as far as I am concerned, been reached today," he said.

"With two years to go to the single currency deadline, it is surprising that there have not been talks on the overvaluation of European currencies versus the dollar. Without this we will have serious problems bringing this monetary union process to fruition and, above all, big problems managing the single currency afterwards," Gerard said.

"The Germans must take account of the differences between our countries, acknowledge that our interests must be defended and that our country faces a difficult social and political situation with the undervaluation of the dollar.
